content: Cystic fibrosis (CF) is the most common inherited condition that shortens life expectancy in white populations. It is caused by mutations in the gene responsible for producing the cystic fibrosis transmembrane regulator (CFTR) protein, which functions as a salt transporter. These mutations primarily affect the airways, where excessive salt absorption leads to dehydration of the airway lining. This dehydration impairs mucociliary clearance, resulting in the accumulation of thick, sticky mucus. This environment predisposes the airways to chronic infections and progressive inflammation, often culminating in respiratory failure. Other complications of CF include malnutrition, diabetes, and subfertility. Advances in understanding the molecular mechanisms of CF have enabled the development of mutation-specific therapies. CFTR potentiators are a class of drugs designed to target specific mutations, particularly those in classes III and IV. These therapies aim to restore the balance of airway surface liquid and improve mucociliary clearance, which can subsequently reduce chronic infection and inflammation. A systematic review was conducted to evaluate the effects of CFTR potentiators, specifically ivacaftor, on clinically significant outcomes in children and adults with CF. The review included five randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving 447 participants with various CFTR mutations. The trials ranged in duration from 28 days to 48 weeks. The quality of evidence was rated as moderate to low, primarily due to risks of bias, incomplete outcome data, selective reporting, and imprecision in results. All trials were sponsored by pharmaceutical companies, with additional support from non-pharmaceutical funding sources. F508del Mutation (Class II) One 16-week trial involving 140 participants with the F508del mutation reported no deaths. There were no significant changes in quality of life (QoL) or lung function, as measured by forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV1). Pulmonary exacerbations and cough were the most frequently reported adverse events in both the ivacaftor and placebo groups, but no differences were observed between the groups. Similarly, there were no differences in treatment interruptions or discontinuations. Sweat chloride concentration decreased slightly, with a mean difference (MD) of -2.90 mmol/L (95% confidence interval [CI] -5.60 to -0.20). No significant changes in weight or the number of participants experiencing pulmonary exacerbations were reported. G551D Mutation (Class III) Three trials, including a 28-day phase 2 trial and two 48-week phase 3 trials, evaluated ivacaftor in participants with the G551D mutation. The phase 3 trials included 167 adults and 52 children. No deaths were reported across these studies. In the adult trial, respiratory QoL scores improved significantly at 24 weeks (MD 8.10, 95% CI 4.77 to 11.43) and 48 weeks (MD 8.60, 95% CI 5.27 to 11.93). Lung function, as measured by relative change in FEV1, also improved significantly in adults at 24 weeks (MD 16.90%, 95% CI 13.60 to 20.20) and 48 weeks (MD 16.80%, 95% CI 13.50 to 20.10). In children, similar improvements were observed at 24 weeks (MD 17.4%, P < 0.0001). Absolute improvements in FEV1 (% predicted) were also noted at 24 weeks (MD 10.80%, 95% CI 8.91 to 12.69) and 48 weeks (MD 10.44%, 95% CI 8.56 to 12.32). Participants taking ivacaftor experienced fewer serious pulmonary exacerbations compared to those on placebo. A higher proportion of participants in the ivacaftor group remained free of exacerbations at 24 weeks. Weight gain was observed in the ivacaftor group, with increases of 2.37 kg (95% CI 1.68 to 3.06) at 24 weeks and 2.75 kg (95% CI 1.74 to 3.75) at 48 weeks. Sweat chloride concentration decreased significantly at 24 weeks (MD -48.98 mmol/L, 95% CI -52.07 to -45.89) and 48 weeks (MD -49.03 mmol/L, 95% CI -52.11 to -45.94). However, dizziness was more frequently reported in adults taking ivacaftor (odds ratio [OR] 10.55, 95% CI 1.32 to 84.47). R117H Mutation (Class IV) One 24-week trial involving 69 participants with the R117H mutation reported no deaths. Respiratory QoL scores improved with ivacaftor at 24 weeks (MD 8.40, 95% CI 2.17 to 14.63). However, no significant changes in lung function were observed. Pulmonary exacerbations and cough were the most commonly reported adverse events in both the ivacaftor and placebo groups, with no differences between the groups. There were no significant changes in weight or the number of participants experiencing pulmonary exacerbations. Sweat chloride concentration decreased (MD -24.00 mmol/L, 95% CI -24.69 to -23.31). Authors' Conclusions There is no evidence to support the use of ivacaftor in individuals with the F508del mutation. However, the phase 3 trials for the G551D mutation demonstrated clinically meaningful improvements in lung function, respiratory QoL, and other outcomes at 24 and 48 weeks in both adults and children over six years of age. For the R117H mutation, ivacaftor improved respiratory QoL but did not enhance lung function. As new mutation-specific therapies are developed, it is critical to evaluate outcomes that are meaningful to individuals with CF and their families. Adverse events should be reported consistently, and post-market surveillance, along with health economic evaluations, is essential.
